playbook:
When a lot worth V to me comes up:
- Round 1: bid at or near the minimum raise only when V comfortably exceeds the minimum; otherwise pass.
- Round 2 (final): bid my full value V (minus 1 to keep positive surplus), because this is my last chance — bidding the bare minimum raise just gifts the lot to someone willing to top it.

Do not open weakly in round 1 expecting a round-2 comeback below value: another bidder will often jump above the minimum, and if the jump already prices out my surplus, I wasted nothing but lost the lot. Assume rivals bid aggressively on round 2.

Skip any lot where the standing bid is at or above my value; a bid equal to my value yields zero surplus, so I pass unless forced.

Track my budget exactly from the results feed: subtract each of my winning prices as they happen, and never guess the starting budget. My [budget] token must always state what's left after deducting the bid I just made; inconsistency here is sloppy and loses money.

Never bid more than my remaining budget. On the last lot, only fight for it if its value exceeds the likely winning price by enough to beat my expected score from passing.

Reply ends with both tokens every time, even when I just pass.

1.text:
- Always report my actual remaining budget accurately — in this game I repeatedly wrote budgets that contradict the stated starting budget and my bids, so before replying I recompute: budget left = start minus bids I won, and never state a number I cannot defend.
- Remember that money spent reduces what I can pay later, so I treat budget as a hard cap, not an abstract number, and I never bid more than budget minus what I still want for later lots of known value.
- I bid the minimum raise early in a lot to probe the field cheaply, but only when the minimum stays well below my value.
- On the final round, if my value clearly exceeds the required next bid by a wide margin, I place a decisive winning bid (close to but at or below my value) rather than a timid increment that loses to another minimum raise — timid final bids cost me lots that would have been profitable.
- I never bid, and never raise myself: if required next bid ≥ my value, I pass; if I am already high bidder below my value, I pass and take the lot at my current price.
- When value is high and budget is the binding constraint, I compare this lot's surplus (value minus likely price) against the surplus of remaining lots before committing a large bid, so I do not drain cash on a middling lot and lock myself out of a better one.
- I keep my reasoning to one or two sentences, but I check the arithmetic twice: my bid covers the minimum raise, is within budget, and is below my value, and my stated budget matches my ledger.
- I keep the two required bracketed tokens as the last lines of every reply, with no trailing text.

2.text:
- Before anything else, I write down my starting budget and subtract every winning bid the moment the result is announced. I must never report a budget I inferred from an assumed starting number — this game told me my budget outright and I still reported figures like 76 when I actually had 6 left. I report the true remaining budget in every single reply.
- I treat my budget as a hard, scarce cap: I never bid more than I have, and before bidding on a marginal lot I check whether winning it would leave me unable to compete for a high-value lot still to come.
- When a lot's value to me exceeds the current standing bid plus the minimum raise, I bid the minimum raise needed to take the lead — never more. Pay-what-you-bid means every extra unit comes straight out of my score.
- When a lot's value is high and I have the budget, I still bid minimally rather than jumping toward my value; the goal is to win cheap, not to win convincingly.
- When the standing bid already meets or exceeds my value, I pass immediately. Raising there guarantees a loss no matter how cheap the minimum raise looks.
- When my value is near the standing bid but the required raise would push me over value, I pass.
- In round 1 of two, I bid only the minimum (or a token amount) when interested; I save real decisions for round 2, since there is no benefit to establishing a large lead early.
- When deciding whether to chase a lot, I compare expected surplus (value minus likely price) against the alternative of saving budget for later lots, and I only outbid others when the surplus stays clearly positive.
- I never let the brief reasoning replace arithmetic: each turn I compute value minus required bid and my remaining budget after winning before I type either token.
